 I.      INTRODUCTION.

        The Administrative Law Judges correctly recommended Route 894, the route identified by

the Applicants and supported by the record, as the route that best balances the Commission’s

routing criteria. The Exceptions (Exceptions) to the Proposal for Decision (PFD) include

significant link-specific avoidance requests but do not demonstrate that a competing route achieves

a better overall balance.

        If the Commission nevertheless declines to approve Route 894, the record supports Route

899, Commission Staff’s Route 487, or the northern Routes 392 and 410 as the strongest

alternatives. These routes are materially better alternatives than Routes 296, 296 Option A, 572,

or CCG. Those latter routes do not improve the overall balance achieved by Route 894 and instead

introduce significant routing deficiencies, including, for Route 296, proximity to tabulated

Habitable Structures such as the Florence Elementary School and the Lawler Baptist Church,

together with the engineering and environmental constraints discussed herein.

        This Reply therefore defends the Administrative Law Judges’ (ALJs) selection of Route

894, explains why Routes 899, 487, 392, and 410 provide reasonable fallback positions, and

addresses why the Commission should reject Routes 296, 296 Option A, 572, and CCG.1

          The Exceptions mistake the Administrative Law Judges’ candidly sympathetic description

of the route selection process as choosing the “least bad” option for a lack of analysis. The ALJs

did not simply announce a result; instead, they identified the four routes on which the parties

principally focused, compared them on cost, length, Habitable Structures, compatible right-of-

way, park and recreational impacts, riparian areas, and historical and cultural resources, and then

evaluated the principal route-specific concerns developed at the hearing.2

         The ALJs determined that Route 894 is the best route because it provides the strongest

route-wide balance of the Commission’s routing criteria. It affects only 85 Habitable Structures,

the lowest count among the Focus Routes. They found Route 894 remains among the more cost-

effective alternatives and that cost and length did not materially distinguish the Focus Routes;3 that

Routes 296 and 392 performed materially worse than Routes 487 and 894 on Prudent Avoidance;

that Route 296 placed the project within 500 feet of Florence Elementary School and two church

buildings belonging to the Lawler Baptist Church; and that Route 392 affected substantially more

Habitable Structures and cultural resources.4 The ALJs then directly compared Routes 487 and

894, recognizing Route 487’s greater paralleling but also its incrementally greater impact on parks

and recreational areas, noting Route 894 has 0.00 miles of its length within 1,000 feet of a park or

recreational area.5

II.     REPLY TO ROUTES 296, 572 AND CCG.7

        Some of the Exceptions urge the Commission to select Route 296, Route 296-Western

Mod, Route 572 or Route CCG. These requests favor using Link J31 to cross the Colorado River.

As will be discussed, Link J31 is not the best option to cross the Colorado River. To use Link J31,

the project must necessarily pass through the Link G6-I1-J31-J32-J33 sequence. These links

present the concerns discussed below, and in the case of Route 296, include additional issues raised

by the Link F33-F34-F6-F7-G31 sequence. Routes using Link J31 sacrifice Route 894’s distinct

advantages in cost, Habitable Structures, environmental impacts, river exposure, stream crossings,

recorded historical and archeological sites, Prudent Avoidance, and route-wide moderation, in

order to move the Colorado River crossing incrementally farther south of two state parks. That

trade-off is not supported by the full record.

 A. Community Values.

        The record shows that community values in these proceedings include residences, schools,

historical and archeological concerns, churches, ranching operations, local land use, public

concerns, and environmental resources.8 Route 894 honors these values. Route 894 affects 85

Habitable Structures; Route CCG affects 105; Route 572 affects 107; and Route 296 affects 105,

one of which is the Florence Elementary School and two of which are Lawler Baptist Church

buildings.9 Route 296 is especially problematic under Community Values because of its use of

the Link F33-F34-F6-F7-G31 sequence.10 Notably, Florence Elementary School at Link F34 is

a daily gathering place for children, teachers, staff, and families, and Florence ISD reminds us that

schools are community resources for education, sporting events, public meetings, and recreation.11

Moreover, Florence Elementary School has capacity to grow to 740 students as residential

development occurs.12 Link F34 also affects two Habitable Structures identified as church

buildings.13

        The southerly routes also fare poorly on Community Values because they impact the third

highest ranked community concern – historical and archeological sites. Routes like CCG, 572 and

296 (all of which use Link J31) cross significant historical and archeological sites, including four

sites assigned Smithsonian Trinomial designations, namely Trinomials 41BT366, 41BT562,

41BT566 and 41BT567, all assigned by the Texas Archeological Research Laboratory in

cooperation with the Texas Historical Commission.14 These Trinomials are expansive, most

         2.       Reply to the Claimed Pipeline Paralleling Advantage.

        Some Exceptions erroneously fault the PFD for failing to utilize an alleged paralleling

advantage at Link J31. Applicants’ witness, Brenda Perkins, confirmed that they did not credit

pipeline paralleling as compatible right-of-way.31 Moreover, the record shows that Link J31 does

not “abut” a pipeline – it is at least 1,200 feet away from a pipeline that was bored under the

Colorado River.32 Applicants’ discovery responses confirm that “paralleling” means routing two

linear features so they are the same distance from one another at any given point, and that the

maximum distance of separation used to make “paralleling” determinations was approximately

“100 feet from the edge of the abutting right-of-way.”33 Ms. Reinecke admitted that the pipeline

“crossing” the Colorado River was actually bored under the Colorado River and that the pipe ran

“hundreds of feet below the top of [the] bluffs” located at the banks of the Colorado River.34 She

also confirmed that the pipeline began its descent 100-200 feet before it even got to the river

banks.35 Thus, this distance and subsurface alignment of the pipeline do not establish a previously

disturbed corridor at Link J31.

        A fair assessment of the record shows that only one Colorado River crossing “parallels”

anything at all – in this case, an existing electric transmission line along Link U3, a component of

Routes 392 and 410. Thus, the existing-infrastructure argument more directly supports routes

using Link U3 than routes using Link J31.

         Docket No. 37448 demonstrates the importance of considering recreational and aesthetic

impacts, but it does not establish that Route 894 should be rejected. The previous Commission

denied that application, so it did not approve the earlier ALJs’ recommended Route GN6.37 The

         Notably, the river crossings in Docket No. 37448 and this Docket are materially different.

As the Colorado River Alliance explained, former Link C20 was near present Link J26, not Link

to treat Docket 37448 as an endorsement of Link J31.

 C.      Aesthetic and historical values; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C).

        1.       Aesthetics.

        The Exceptions raise three broad criticisms of the ALJs’ treatment of aesthetics. These

criticisms do not provide a sufficient basis to defeat the PFD. First, several landowners argue

that the analysis understates the aesthetic harm experienced from private property, citing how

views from homes, ranch headquarters, overlooks, riverfront areas, native pastures, and working

ranches would be impacted. Second, the Exceptions criticize the traditional framework used to

measure aesthetics because it focuses primarily on visibility from public locations, including

highways, roads, parks, and recreational areas. Third, the Exceptions criticize the PFD for not

following a pre-application recommendation by TPWD to apply a broad 5-mile buffer for the

parks. Given the constraints of the study area, this 5-mile buffer was not practical, so instead, the

Applicants evaluated parks and recreational areas under the Commission’s standard routing

metrics, including whether a route crosses a park or recreational area, whether a park or

recreational area is located within 1,000 feet of the route centerline, and whether right-of-way lies

within the one-half-mile foreground visual zone of a public park or recreational area.46

        Notably, the PFD treats aesthetics as one component of the overall routing balance, not as

a stand-alone basis for selecting Route 894. The PFD properly relies on objective, publicly

measurable indicators. On those measures, Route 894 performs best or nearly best among the

Focus Routes. Among all routes, the number of parks or recreational areas within 1,000 feet

ranged from zero to three, and the range of right-of-way within a park or recreational foreground

           These criticisms do not overcome Route 894’s objective advantages. The Commission

must compare complete routes using consistent measures rather than allow each party’s description

comparing complete routes. While the PFD does not find cultural and historical values as the

deciding factor, the PFD’s findings favor Route 894 over Route 296 and especially Route 392 on

six fewer recorded resources within 1,000 feet.53 Thus, the PFD’s cultural and historical analysis
